title: Quantum Generative Models of Mid-Price Movement in Limit Order Books
journal_or_venue: ICAIF '24: 5th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (Proceedings)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a quantum-channel based generative model (quantum hidden Markov model / unitary QHMM) for directional mid-price movements in limit order books, modeling observations as measurements of an emission system entangled with a hidden quantum state. It describes parameterization via quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements, provides analytical expressions for sequence probabilities, presents a learning algorithm including model-order estimation and evolutionary optimization, and demonstrates training and small-scale quantum hardware experiments on real LOB data.
methodology_description: The authors modelled directional mid-price movements in limit order books (LOBs) as a stochastic process language and proposed a quantum generative modelling approach based on Quantum Hidden Markov Models (QHMMs). They parameterized QHMMs as unitary quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurement (Unitary QHMMs): a hidden-state Hilbert space (ℋ_S) entangled with an emission qubit (ℋ_E). Empirical sequence distributions were estimated from observed binary directional returns (y_t = 1 if mid-price return > 0 else 0) and represented via finite-length sequence probabilities and Hankel matrices; low-rank Hankel approximations were used to control model complexity. Learning/search over the space of circuit structures and continuous gate parameters was performed by a memetic evolutionary algorithm that combines a global evolutionary (population-based) search over circuit structures with local Metropolis-annealing search and non-linear parametric optimization of gate parameters. The fitness objective was the negative average variational distance between empirical and model sequence distributions up to a fixed length. Models (typically with a 3-qubit hidden register + 1 emission qubit = 4 physical qubits in circuit) were trained on both event-level and 1-second-aggregated LOB data for AMZN and GOOGL. Trained circuits were transpiled and optimized for execution on real hardware; error suppression/mitigation techniques (dynamical decoupling, Pauli twirling) were applied for QPU runs, and hardware outputs were compared to target distributions.
algorithms_used: Unitary QHMM (quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurement)
Non-linear parametric optimization (per-structure gate parameter optimization)
Hankel matrix rank estimation and low-rank approximation
experimental_setup: Models were trained in simulation (Qiskit) and selected trained circuits were transpiled and executed on IBM Eagle r3 QPU. Circuits typically used 4 physical qubits (3-qubit hidden state + 1 emission qubit). Learning used a population-based evolutionary process (μ=200 parents, offspring size λ = γ·μ adaptive) for up to 300 generations or until fitness threshold met; sequence distributions up to length 10 were used for training. Transpilation and multi-stage optimization reduced 2-qubit depth (example reductions from 100/110 to 53/86). Error suppression via dynamical decoupling and Pauli twirling was applied for hardware runs.
dataset_used: Event-level limit order book data for AMZN (Amazon.com Inc.) on 2022-06-03 (T = 102,418 events) and GOOGL (Alphabet Inc.) on 2022-07-19 (T = 235,928 events). Additionally, 1-second aggregated versions were created by taking the last mid-price in each one-second interval.

Iterate evolutionary optimization for up to 300 generations: select parents, generate offspring via structure-modifying operators (Modify), apply local Metropolis annealing, and perform per-structure continuous gate-parameter optimization (memetic step) to maximize fitness.

[supported] Low-rank Hankel approximations permit small quantum models to approximate longer sequence statistics: e.g., 3-qubit models approximate up to length ~14 (1s-aggregated) / ~16 (event-level) at ~1% approximation error; 5-qubit models reach ~20 / ~22 respectively.

[supported] The learning procedure combining evolutionary/metaheuristic search and local optimization successfully produced circuit ansätze that match empirical finite-sequence distributions for the studied datasets.

[supported] Trained circuits were transpiled and run on IBM Eagle r3 hardware for short sequences (3 time steps); hardware output distributions showed reasonable agreement with the target distributions with increased variance for deeper circuits/noisier runs.

[supported] Practical circuit compilation required reducing two-qubit gate depth substantially (examples: unoptimized depths ~100–110 two-qubit layers reduced to ~53–86 through multi-stage transpilation and optimization).

[speculative] QHMM models capture short-term dependencies via entanglement between hidden and emission systems; they can model non-Markovian-looking observation processes while the underlying state evolution remains Markovian.

results_summary: The authors propose and implement a unitary-circuit parameterized Quantum Hidden Markov Model (QHMM) to generatively model mid-price directional movements in limit order books. They estimate model order via Hankel-rank analysis and use evolutionary/metaheuristic optimization to fit circuit parameters to empirical finite-sequence distributions for AMZN and GOOGL event-level and 1-second-aggregated data. Small quantum models (3 qubits) achieved very low empirical variational distance (<1e-4) for sequence lengths up to 10; with low-rank approximation, 3- and 5-qubit models can approximate longer sequence statistics (up to mid-20s in length under a 1% error threshold). Trained circuits were compiled and executed on IBM hardware for short sequences, showing reasonable agreement with target distributions after error suppression and transpiler optimizations. The work emphasizes theoretical parsimony and analytic tractability of QHMMs but does not present a direct empirical comparison to classical HMMs or other classical generative models.
performance_claims: Variational distance between model and target distributions optimized to values less than 1e-4 for sequences up to length 10 using 3-qubit models.
Datasets: AMZN (102,418 events), GOOGL (235,928 events) used for training/testing.
3-qubit models accurately define probabilities of sequences up to length ~10 (direct rank), and under 1% approximation error (low-rank) up to length ~14 (1s-aggregated) and ~16 (event-level).
5-qubit models (low-rank approx) can approximate sequence probabilities up to lengths ~20 (1s-aggregated) and ~22 (event-level) at 1% error.
Evolutionary training setup: parent population size mu=200, up to 300 generations, offspring size lambda adaptive (gamma * mu), stopping criterion fitness > -1e-4.
Circuit compilation: unoptimized two-qubit depths ~100 and ~110 for two circuits reduced to ~53 and ~86 after multi-stage transpilation and optimization.
Hardware runs produced distribution histograms for 3-symbol sequences showing good agreement with targets, with increased variance for deeper circuits (no quantitative fidelity number reported).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper cites and relies on a theoretical result (from prior work) that QHMMs can offer quadratic state-space parsimony compared to classical HMMs (n -> sqrt(n)). This advantage is presented as a theoretical property; the present work demonstrates feasibility on small empirical datasets but does not provide a direct empirical comparison showing a practical quantum advantage over classical models.
limitations: Inferring the rank of the Hankel matrix from data is undecidable (author-cited).

The empirical Hankel rank grows approximately exponentially with sequence length, suggesting the underlying process may be non-finite-state and limiting exact finite-dimensional modeling (author-observed).
Longer sequences occur with low frequency; probabilities for long sequences cannot be reliably estimated from finite samples (author-stated).
Finite-rank approximations require choosing a cutoff (number of singular values) and induce approximation error that must be traded off against model dimension (author-discussed).
Hardware noise introduces variance in the modeled distributions; deeper circuits produce larger deviations from the ideal model (author-observed in hardware runs).

Circuit depth and qubit connectivity requirements are high after transpilation; optimization reduced depth but not enough in some cases, constraining hardware implementation (author-experiment result).

The study models only the binary directional mid-price movement (up/down) and therefore omits other LOB information such as magnitudes, volumes, multi-level book state, and timestamps (author-specified modeling choice).
